title: Chapter 121 — Leading the Trade Desk and The Multi-Engine Floor
intro: The trade desk as a business unit and managing the specialist alongside the retail team.

sections.title: The Trade Desk Is a Different Business
sections.content:
The trade desk — serving builders, contractors, designers, and property managers — operates differently from the retail floor. Longer sales cycles, relationship-driven decisions, volume pricing, project coordination.

Managing both the retail floor and the trade desk requires treating them as two distinct business units with different KPIs, different rhythms, and different coaching needs.

The mistake is applying retail metrics to trade salespeople or vice versa. A trade salesperson might work one deal for three months and close a $200,000 project. Measuring their weekly closing ratio against the floor team makes no sense.

sections.title: The Multi-Engine Floor
sections.content:
The strongest stores have multiple revenue engines running simultaneously: retail walk-ins, trade accounts, online sales, kitchen packages, and replacement-cycle follow-ups.

Managing all of these requires different people with different skills — or the same people with clear processes for each channel. Either way, the manager needs to understand all the engines and know which ones need attention.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating trade and multi-engine management, ask:

Is the trade desk being measured with appropriate KPIs — not retail metrics?
Does the manager understand the different rhythms of trade vs. retail selling?
Are all revenue engines being managed — or is the team only focused on walk-in traffic?
